claims.text: Pulumi has introduced a new feature, component state migrations, that lets component authors ship the upgrade path together with the component itself.

A Pulumi component state migration translates the saved state of a component and its children before Pulumi works out which resources need to change, so component authors can change a component's internal design and include the migration in the same release.
The Pulumi component state migrations API is experimental and may change.
A GitHub discussion for feedback on component state migrations exists at https://github.com/pulumi/pulumi/discussions/24799.

Pulumi components let you group resources into a reusable building block (network, database, application service) that can be shared across projects and teams, with consumers working only with inputs and outputs.
The legacy AWSX VPC component manages the VPC, subnets, route tables, and gateways behind a few lines of code.
A Pulumi docs page exists at /docs/iac/guides/building-extending/components/state-migrations/ covering the component state migrations callback contract.
The pulumi/examples repository contains the example directory aws-ts-awsx-vpc-state-migration with three programs (v1, v2, v3) and the migration code.

The v1 program of the AWSX VPC state-migration example uses the legacy `awsx.classic.ec2.Vpc` component, which creates a VPC with one isolated subnet, a route table and its association, and an internet gateway.
In the v1 example, a security group sits outside the VPC component and refers to the VPC.

Without a migration connecting old state to new code, upgrading could replace the VPC instead of keeping it, and because the security group refers to the VPC's ID, a new VPC would mean replacing the security group too (per the linked AWS CloudFormation EC2 SecurityGroup VpcId documentation).
The AWSX VPC state-migration example does not create a database.
If a database has to be recreated, its replacement does not automatically contain the old data, and without a backup or data migration deleting the old database could mean losing that data.
The v2 program of the example upgrades to the modern `awsx.ec2.Vpc` component while keeping the existing network.
The v3 program of the example removes AWSX and declares the VPC, subnet, route table, association, and internet gateway directly with `@pulumi/aws`, with Pulumi still managing them.

Across all three versions of the example, the AWS resource IDs stay the same and the security group continues to use the same VPC; only how Pulumi records the resources and their relationships changes.

In the example, the v1 resource tree is `awsx:x:ec2:Vpc "vpc"` containing `aws:ec2/vpc:Vpc "vpc"`, an `awsx:x:ec2:Subnet "vpc-isolated-0"` (with child Subnet, RouteTable, RouteTableAssociation), and an `awsx:x:ec2:InternetGateway "vpc"` (with child InternetGateway).

In the example, the v2 resource tree is `awsx:ec2:Vpc "vpc"` containing `aws:ec2/vpc:Vpc "vpc"`, with subnet "vpc-isolated-1" (route table and association nested beneath it) and internet gateway "vpc" as children of the VPC.
In the example, the v3 resource tree has `aws:ec2/vpc:Vpc "vpc"` as root with subnet "vpc-isolated-1" (route table and association nested beneath) and internet gateway "vpc" as children.

Pulumi's state records both physical resources and the components that group them; each record has a Pulumi name called a URN, and managed resources also have an ID from the cloud provider such as an AWS VPC ID.
The legacy AWSX VPC component wraps the subnet and internet gateway in separate components, while modern AWSX removes those wrappers and puts the managed resources under different parents.
In the example, the Pulumi name of the subnet changes from `vpc-isolated-0` (legacy AWSX) to `vpc-isolated-1` (modern AWSX).

Pulumi aliases handle changes to a resource's name, type, or parent when its saved state remains compatible, but they do not by themselves remove component wrappers and transfer references to replacement resources, which a state migration does together.
A Pulumi component registers a state migration by passing a migration callback through the `stateMigrations` resource option, together with an alias for the legacy component type.
The example's `migrateClassicVpc` function lives in aws-ts-awsx-vpc-state-migration/v2/migration.ts in pulumi/examples.
A state migration callback receives the saved state of the aliased old component followed by the state of its children; the alias lets Pulumi find the old component.

A state migration callback returns `newState` (the complete set of records that should replace the old component and its children) and `successors` (a map from each old URN that disappears to the URN that takes its place).

In the example migration callback, initial checks make it safe to run again (if state already uses modern AWSX or plain AWS resources it does nothing), and an unexpected component type raises an error instead of guessing.
The example's `rename` helper copies the saved record and changes its URN, type, and parent, preserving the AWS resource ID and other saved fields, and moves the subnet under the managed VPC.

The Pulumi engine uses the `successors` mappings to update dependencies and resource references elsewhere in the stack, so that the security group's reference to the VPC remains valid after migration and stays connected to the migrated VPC record with the same AWS VPC ID.
In the example, the two subnet entries in `successors` tell the Pulumi engine that the old component wrapper and the managed subnet both point to the same new subnet record.

The example's second migration (v3/migration.ts) removes the AWSX VPC component record and moves the managed VPC into its place; both the old component and its VPC child map to the new VPC record, and the VPC keeps its AWS ID while other resources remain beneath it.
In the example's v3 program, the plain VPC registration keeps aliases for both previous component types (legacy and modern AWSX) and both migration callbacks.
Pulumi runs multiple state migration callbacks in order, passing each result to the next callback.
A stack still using legacy AWSX can upgrade directly to the plain AWS version, and a stack already using modern AWSX skips the first migration.
Once both migrations have run, both callbacks return no result on later updates.
Keeping earlier migrations with the component means users can skip versions without editing stack state by hand.
After a state migration changes saved state, Pulumi compares the new program with that state and calls the provider for any remaining changes.
In the example, keeping resource IDs does not guarantee an empty preview: the example can still show in-place updates for provider defaults and tags.
To try the example, start with `v1` and follow its README, using the same stack, backend, project name, AWS region, and availability zone for each version.

When upgrading between the example versions, `pulumi preview` should show no creates, deletes, or replacements for the existing VPC, subnet, route table, association, internet gateway, and security group.
`pulumi preview` evaluates a state migration without saving it, and `pulumi up` (the update) saves the migrated state.

When a component author registers a state migration inside the component implementation, users do not need to write the migration, attach the callback, or edit their stack state; Pulumi runs the migration as part of the normal preview and update after they upgrade the component.
For an internal component change that keeps the same inputs and outputs, users can keep their existing component calls without knowing which resources moved or how saved state changed.
Pulumi state migration callbacks (the state migrations resource option for components) run during both previews and updates when prior state exists for the resource.
Pulumi state migration callbacks must be idempotent.
A Pulumi state migration callback must return no result when the resource's state no longer needs migration.
Pulumi state migration callbacks rewrite resource state without performing provider operations.

A Pulumi component state migration (the `stateMigrations` resource option callback) is a pure function that transforms the saved state of a component and its children into the state expected by a new component version.
A component state migration callback returns the updated state records and successor mappings.
In a component state migration result, each successor mapping connects an old URN that is omitted from the returned result to the URN of the returned resource that takes its place.
If no migration is needed, a component state migration callback returns no result.
The option reference page at /docs/iac/concepts/resources/options/statemigrations/ has a 'callback-api' section that explains the component state migration callback API.

Component state migration callback state entries use the Pulumi checkpoint resource format documented in the developer docs deployment schema (pulumi-resource-state), including fields such as `urn`, `type`, `id`, `parent`, `provider`, `inputs`, and `outputs`.
The Pulumi developer docs deployment schema reference at pulumi-developer-docs.readthedocs.io has a 'pulumi-resource-state' section describing the checkpoint resource state format.
A component state migration callback that returns no result can remain attached when using update plans or targeted updates.
The restrictions on state-changing results of component state migrations (when using update plans or targeted updates) do not require removing an already-applied migration.
